name: Fatima Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a farm manager for Vale Agri Services, a contract farming company. Landowners who don't want to farm themselves hire us, and I look after three of their farms: a three-hundred-cow dairy, and two arable places growing maize and grass for silage. I've got six people on my team. Most of my day is in the pickup between the three, checking the cows, the silage clamps and the crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you're best at?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting the silage right. Cut at the right moment, clamped tight, sheeted well, and the cows milk all winter. Last year we had the best silage analysis in the company, and I've got the printout on the fridge. My husband Lukas is a mechanic at the tractor dealer, so he fixes what my crew breaks, which is handy and also a source of arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for paperwork and that's it. I'd say that at the company's managers' day and maybe in our village group chat if someone brought it up. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on. I'd keep using the chat program to write the monthly reports to the landowners, because that saves me a good Sunday afternoon each month. The rest of my job is weather and cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep the savings going at about two hundred and fifty a month, and I'd keep pushing the company for a better pickup, because mine's got two hundred thousand kilometres on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the chat program for reports. When did you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year ago, after another manager showed me at the managers' day. I watched her do a report in ten minutes that takes me two hours. I tried it the next week. That's usually how I do things, see it work, then try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd want from AI that didn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good weather forecast for silage cutting. Three dry days in May is the whole year for us. If a computer could tell me that properly, I'd pay for it myself.

S0.say: I'd tell the company managers' day and the village group chat that AI is useful for paperwork and not much else. Nothing dramatic.
S0.think: I carry on as I am, using the chat program for monthly landowner reports, which saves me a Sunday afternoon. The rest of my job is weather and cows.
S0.do: Keeps saving about two hundred and fifty a month and keeps pushing the company to replace her worn-out pickup. Continues using the chat program for reports.
S0.quote: Three dry days in May is the whole year for us.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is matter-of-fact and proud of her silage. She picked up AI for reports only after watching a colleague use it, which is her pattern. The one thing she'd pay for herself is a reliable forecast for cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible and learn it. I'd say that to my crew straight. And I'd ask the company what their plan is, out loud at the managers' day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think contract farming is exactly where it hits first. Our whole business is doing the work cheaper than the landowner could. If robots make it cheaper still, the company buys robots and cuts crew. I think I'd keep my job, but I'd have to cut two of my six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on whatever course the company offers, and I'd ask for one if there isn't one. I'd use the AI tools more, for planning which fields to cut. And we'd up the savings to three hundred, because Mina's going to want driving lessons soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be fine, probably, but I'd be the one doing the cutting of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want to say names. But the ones who struggle with anything new, and the youngest one, because the company would say he's got time to find something else. I'd fight for the youngest, actually. He's the best with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Lukas's job change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably be busier. Somebody has to fix all these robots, and he's good. That makes me feel safer at home, honestly. One of us gains while the other one's job gets squeezed.

S1.say: I'd tell my crew straight that it's coming, so let's be sensible and learn it. At the managers' day I'd ask the company out loud what its plan is.
S1.think: Contract farming gets hit first because our whole business is doing the work cheaper. I'd probably keep my job but have to cut two of my six.
S1.do: Goes on the company's training course or asks for one, uses AI tools for planning which fields to cut, and raises savings to three hundred a month ahead of her daughter's driving lessons.
S1.feel: Uneasy, because she'd likely be fine but would have to let people go.
S1.quote: I think I'd keep my job, but I'd have to cut two of my six.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima understands her company's business model and sees why it would move fast. Her unease is about being the one who lets people go. Her husband's mechanic job is a hedge she named herself, which lowers her own worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should help companies phase it in, maybe with some money for the people who lose out. I'm not a campaigner, but I'd say it if asked. In the village chat I'd probably just share what's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's at risk too. A robot that can run silage and milk cows doesn't need six people, and it might not need a manager across three farms either. One person in an office could watch twelve farms. I'm not sure that person is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd ask the company for that office job, before anyone else does. I'd learn every tool they bring in, even on my own time. At home we'd cut the eating out and the summer camp, and put everything we can into savings, maybe five hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight chest, but I'd feel like I can still grab something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one person could watch twelve farms. Why might that not be you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's a man in head office who's younger and does spreadsheets in his sleep. I'm good in a field. I'm only all right on a screen. In two years I'm not sure I can turn that around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is two silage seasons. I can just about learn the new system in that time if I'm lucky and the company backs me. Any less luck than that and I'm out, with Lukas carrying us.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and the government should help companies phase it in, with money for people who lose out. I'm no campaigner, but I'd say it if asked.
S2.think: My own job is at risk, because one person in an office could watch twelve robot-run farms. I'm good in a field and only all right on a screen, so that person might not be me.
S2.do: Asks the company for the office role straight away and learns every new tool, even in her own time. Cuts eating out and the children's summer camp and saves up to five hundred a month.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, but feels she can still grab something.
S2.quote: I'm good in a field. I'm only all right on a screen.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture Fatima moves quickly despite usually waiting, because she can see the one job left standing. She is frank that a younger colleague may beat her to it. Her husband's work keeps this from tipping into alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train people properly, and companies should do it. I'd tell my crew to start learning now. Calm, practical, that's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is about right for me. I'll have watched the first farms do it and learned from their mistakes, and I'll still be the one who knows the cows and the land. I'd still worry about the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a course in farm robotics at the college, evenings, and the company might pay half. I'd make sure my crew all do the basic training. By year three I'd want my job to be managing the machines across my three farms, and I'd tell the company that's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly settled, with a to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew are you most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who's fifty-eight and has milked cows his whole life. He'd retire early if the company gave him something, and he'd deserve it. I'd push for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mina and Elias about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mina's fifteen, she wants to do something with animals. I'd tell her to keep going but learn the tech side too. Elias is eleven and just wants to play football, so I'd let him.

S3.say: I'd tell my crew to start learning now, because five years is enough to train people properly and companies should do it. Calm and practical.
S3.think: Five years suits me, since I'd watch the first farms and learn from their mistakes while still knowing the cows and land. I'd still worry about the crew.
S3.do: Takes an evening farm robotics course at the college with the company paying half, and makes sure the whole crew does basic training. By year three asks to manage the machines across her three farms, and pushes for an early retirement package for Pete.
S3.quote: I'll have watched the first farms do it and learned from their mistakes, and I'll still be the one who knows the cows and the land.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches Fatima's steady style: watch the early movers, then commit. She has a clear role she wants and would ask for it. Her thought for her oldest worker was an exit with dignity rather than retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long run-up, and there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. Farmers have always adapted. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine. I'd be fifty-three and running machines instead of people, which might be easier on the knees. The bit I can't picture is the dairy without anybody in the parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years I'd do nothing special, just keep learning tools as the company brings them in. Around year four I'd do the robotics course. And we'd plan Mina's university around something that isn't easy to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the normal kind of change, just bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Is there anything you'd lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew. Lunch in the tractor shed, Pete's terrible jokes, the youngest lad's music too loud. If it's me and a screen, I'd be lonely, and nobody talks about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lukas's work still be safe after ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. If the robots get good enough to fix each other, then no. But that's further off than ten years, I'd guess. I don't really know.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long run-up with no excuse for being caught out, and farmers have always adapted. I'd keep it practical.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine at fifty-three, running machines instead of people, which might be easier on the knees. I can't picture the dairy with nobody in the parlour.
S4.do: Keeps learning tools as the company brings them in, takes the robotics course around year four, and plans her daughter Mina's university choice around work that's hard to automate.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, as if it's normal change, only bigger.
S4.quote: If it's me and a screen, I'd be lonely, and nobody talks about that.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Fatima expects to come through and treats it as ordinary change. Her main loss would be the people around her, which she raised herself. She was honest that she doesn't know how long her husband's repair work would last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be fighting a younger man for the last job. What would help is the company paying for training before the robots arrive, and a decent package for the people who don't make it across.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the landowners want. They're the ones paying us. If they decide robots are cheaper, it doesn't matter how good my silage is.

headlineQuote: If they decide robots are cheaper, it doesn't matter how good my silage is.
portrait: Fatima Bauer is 43 and manages three farms, a dairy and two silage farms, for a contract farming company, with a team of six and the best silage analysis in the firm pinned to her fridge. She takes up new tools after seeing a colleague use them, already uses AI for monthly reports, and keeps her views practical and mild. She is calm about the plateau, uneasy under steady change because she'd have to cut two of her crew, and anxious about two-year AGI because a younger, screen-savvy colleague might get the one remaining office job. With five or ten years she plans a robotics course and a role running the machines, though she'd miss her crew and her husband Lukas's mechanic job gives the family a hedge.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be competing with a younger colleague for the last job left.
whatWouldHelp: The company paying for training before the robots arrive, and a decent package for workers who don't make it across.
